newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cell phone operators challenge tariff rates.
newsitem.headline: Indian cell phone operators challenge tariff rates.

text.p: Cellular telephone operators asked an Indian court on Tuesday to overturn a government order which they said set prohibitively high tariff rates for calls from basic, fixed-line phones to mobile units.

G.P. Sangal, a spokesman for the Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI), said the trade group filed a petition with the Delhi High Court challenging the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) order.
The January 29 order set tariff rates which Sangal said were far higher than warranted except in the four largest cities -- Bombay, Calcutta, Delhi and Madras.
"This totally takes the business of cellular operators," Sangal said. "This is a very big disincentive to contact anyone on a cellular phone from a fixed-line phone."
Cellular operators, admitted under an economic liberalisation programme, launched their services in 1995, starting with the four "metropolitan" cities.

United News of India (UNI) said the high court on Tuesday rejected the cellular operators' request for a stay on the order, due to take effect on Saturday, and set a hearing for April 3 on COAI's plea.

Sangal said that under the rates set by the order, a phone call from a basic phone to a cellular unit within the same area, or circle, would cost the user of the basic phone about 10 rupees a minute compared with the current 1.4 rupees.
Normal fixed-line charges would remain in force in the four largest cities.

UNI quoted COAI counsel Mukul Rohtagi as telling the high court that the tariff rates would "finish" cellular operators because half of the calls on cellular phones originate from basic phones and the order would discourage such calls.
Rohtagi argued that the DoT was not empowered to pass such an order, and it was up to the new Telecom Regulatory Authority to do so.

The news agency quoted additional solicitor general A.M. Singhvi, representing the government, as telling the court that except in the four largest cities, authorities could not determine whether a call from a basic phone to a cellular phone was local or long-distance.

Singhvi said the government was following the pricing structure common in the rest of the world, including the United States and Europe. He said the Telecom Regulatory Body had not yet been formed and so not set tariffs.
